newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Peruvian general thinks Fujimori knew of murders.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian general thinks Fujimori knew of murders.

text.p: A Peruvian general, freed after accusing top military brass of violating human rights, told an Argentine newspaper he suspected President Alberto Fujimori knew of a notorious murder of 10 students.

Interviewed immediately after his release by presidential amnesty on Saturday, Gen. Rodolfo Robles told the Clarin newspaper he believed Fujimori knew of the so-called La Cantuta crimes in 1992 that involved the murder of 10 university students, allegedly by security forces.

"He is responsible to a great degree, and I have information to that respect. I suspect he knew of the crimes of La Cantuta, which would make him intellectually responsible." The interview was published on Sunday.
Fujimori helped to free Robles, who had been grabbed by security forces and charged with "insurbordination" in response to his accusations of human rights abuses by the military.
But Robles slammed the Fujimori government, saying that it was "wicked" and completely undemocratic.

"Fujimori uses the mechanisms of state to exercise control over the population," said Robles. "He moulds himself a justice system that serves his personal ambition of being re-elected time and time again, but not only to get a third term, but to get a fourth, a fifth term, and to have an autocracy for a very long period."

The general accused Fujimori, his adviser Vladimiro Montesinos and army chief Nicolas Hermoza of being desperate to stay in power to cover up crimes including "all sorts of business. Drug smuggling too."
But Robles said he could not reveal the sources which led him to believe the president was involved in crimes, and said the amnesty law that freed him also bound him to silence.
"The amnesty law prohibits any sort of investigation or accusation," he said.
In Lima, meanwhile, the U.S. ambassador to Peru Sunday praised Robles' release from jail.

"I am delighted that General Robles is free and I think it is a positive step for (human) rights that Peruvians are defended and protected by Peruvians themselves," the U.S. envoy, Dennis Jett, told reporters.
Jett said the United States had been "worried" by Robles' controversial detention by the military 12 days ago after he linked an army death-squad to a bomb attack on a radio station.

Robles' detention provoked a tide of public protest that forced Fujimori to confront the military with a bill overruling the arrest with an amnesty. Congress unanimously approved the bill, which mandated Robles' release for Saturday, on Thursday.
Washington has frequently chided Peru, particularly the army, for its poor human rights record, but has acknowledged improvements in recent years under Fujimori.
